name: WordPress
answer: A content management system (CMS) written in PHP: a ready-made site with an admin area for editors, not a framework to build an app with. For a blog or marketing site it can be simpler than any stack here; we don't rank CMSs.

name: Firebase
answer: Google's backend-as-a-service: a hosted document database (Firestore), sign-in, file storage and functions, used straight from the app. It replaces much of a backend and database; ranking it is planned for a later version.

name: Supabase
answer: A backend-as-a-service built on PostgreSQL: a hosted database with sign-in, storage and an auto-generated API. It replaces much of a backend; ranking it is planned for a later version.

name: Ruby on Rails
answer: A batteries-included web framework for Ruby, similar in spirit to Django and Laravel. Ruby isn't one of the languages we rank yet, so Rails doesn't appear in the result.

name: Bun
answer: A JavaScript runtime, an alternative to Node.js that also bundles, tests and installs packages. It runs most Node.js code, so it counts as the TypeScript / Node.js option here.

name: Deno
answer: A JavaScript and TypeScript runtime from the original creator of Node.js, with TypeScript and a permission system built in. It counts as the TypeScript / Node.js option here.

name: ORM (object-relational mapper)
answer: A library that lets code read and write database rows as objects, so you write less SQL by hand. Examples: Prisma and Drizzle (TypeScript), SQLAlchemy and Django's ORM (Python), Hibernate (Java), Entity Framework (C#). Choosing an ORM is planned for a later version.

name: Prisma
answer: A TypeScript ORM that generates a typed database client from a schema file; works with PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and MongoDB. It sits inside the TypeScript backend, so it doesn't change the stack.

name: Drizzle ORM
answer: A lightweight TypeScript ORM whose queries look like SQL; works with PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite. It sits inside the TypeScript backend, so it doesn't change the stack.

name: SQLAlchemy
answer: The most used Python database toolkit and ORM, often used with FastAPI or Flask (Django has its own ORM). It doesn't change the stack.

name: Server-side rendering (SSR)
answer: The server builds each page's HTML for every request, so pages show fast and search engines read them; the browser then makes them interactive. It's the "Server-rendered" frontend approach in the result.

name: Single-page app (SPA)
answer: An app that loads once and then runs in the browser, fetching data as you click, like a desktop app. It's the "Single-page app" frontend approach in the result; it suits logged-in apps more than pages that search engines must find.

name: Docker
answer: A way to package an app with everything it needs into a container image that runs the same everywhere. Railway, Render, Fly.io and the cloud providers can all run one, so it mostly affects hosting, not the stack.

sources.note: Railway, Render and Fly.io Dockerfile docs, read 2026-11-09

name: Kubernetes
answer: A system for running many containers across many machines, with automatic restarts and scaling. Powerful, but a lot to operate; small teams usually get the same benefits from a platform as a service.

name: GraphQL
answer: A query language for APIs where the client asks for exactly the fields it needs. Every backend here can serve it with a library; it doesn't change which framework fits.

name: Tailwind CSS
answer: A CSS framework of small utility classes used straight in the markup. It works with every frontend here, so it doesn't change the stack.

name: Mobile app frameworks
answer: React Native, Expo and Flutter build the phone app itself. This tool picks what runs behind it (choose "Backend for a mobile app"); ranking mobile frameworks is planned for a later version.

name: Flask
answer: A minimal Python web framework. We rank FastAPI as the minimal Python option and Django as the batteries-included one; Flask sits close to FastAPI.
